digest.top_line: Salvage RT + ADT: RTOG 9601 bicalutamide OS HR 1.13 at pre-SRT PSA <0.7 vs 0.45 at >1.5; author argues against routine ADT with early SRT.
digest.tldr: No new trial readouts today, only reviews and planning guides. Prostate leads: pre-SRT PSA predicts ADT benefit with salvage RT, and 60 Gy/20 fx is the preferred moderate hypofx schedule, backed by 5-yr non-inferiority in CHHiP, PROFIT and NRG Oncology 0415. Also: target volumes for H&N PNI and seminoma, and a case of hemidiaphragm paralysis after lung SABR (phrenic-area Dmax 57.7 Gy).

sites.intro: Seminoma planning review: para-aortic 20 Gy/10 fx for stage I, superior border lowered to the top of T12.

studies.name: Radiotherapy treatment planning for testicular seminoma
studies.tldr: Review recommends para-aortic 20 Gy/10 fx (stage I), modified dog-leg plus 10 Gy or 16 Gy boost (IIA/IIB), superior border top of T12.
details: 🔍 Evidence-based narrative review (Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 2012); no new outcome data
🔍 85% of seminoma pts present clinical stage I, 11% clinical stage II
🔍 Stage I: surveillance preferred if compliant; adjuvant RT reserved for the minority choosing treatment

rows: Stage IA/IB/IS, no prior pelvic/scrotal surgery
Modified dog-leg 20 Gy/10 fx + 10 Gy/5 fx boost
Modified dog-leg 20 Gy/10 fx + 16 Gy/8 fx boost

details.text: 🔍 Field border changes and their evidence base
subdetails: Superior border: top of T11 → top of T12 (all fields)
Bruns: no relapses in the cranially reduced volume, 80 pts, median f/u 7.1 yrs
Paly nodal mapping, 69 stage II pts: no positive nodes above L1
Dog-leg inferior border: obturator foramen → top of acetabulum
German cohort, 87 pts: no pelvic relapses with acetabular inferior border
CTV1: IVC + 1.2 cm, aorta + 1.9 cm (lateroaortic nodes), excluding bone and bowel
Stage II: ipsilateral iliac vessels + 1.2 cm added to CTV1, down to top of acetabulum
CTV2: GTV + 0.8 cm; PTV = CTV + 0.5 cm
Block edge: PTV + 0.7 cm for penumbra
2D alternative: 2-cm margin on adenopathy to block edge

details: 🔗 TE18: 20 Gy/10 fx not inferior to 30 Gy/15 fx; less lethargy, faster return to work
🔗 TE10: para-aortic vs dog-leg fields → less acute toxicity, faster sperm count recovery
⚠️ AP-PA favored over 7-field IMRT: lower kidney, liver, bowel Dmean despite worse marrow sparing
⚠️ 45% second-cancer reduction from field shrinkage is a linear dose-response model prediction, not observed
studies.significance: The parameters that transfer: superior border at top of T12 (no positive nodes above L1 among 69 mapped stage II pts), dog-leg inferior border at top of acetabulum (no pelvic relapses in 87 pts), and a vascular CTV of IVC + 1.2 cm and aorta + 1.9 cm. Each trims kidney, stomach or bowel dose.
studies.monday_clinic: In clinical stage IIA/IIB seminoma with no prior pelvic or scrotal surgery, this supports modified dog-leg fields bounded at the top of T12 and the top of the acetabulum; it does not extend to pts with horseshoe kidney, inflammatory bowel disease or prior RT, where the source prefers chemotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Evidence-based narrative review with clinical pathways for **clinical stage IA through IIB** seminoma. No systematic search or new outcome data described in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Stage I: **para-aortic 20 Gy/10 fx**, no scrotal RT, clamshell shield, no routine weekly CBC (G2 leukopenia 2%, G3 0 with 20 Gy). Stage IIA/IIB: **modified dog-leg 20 Gy/10 fx** then AP-PA cone-down of **10 Gy/5 fx (IIA) or 16 Gy/8 fx (IIB)**. PTV coverage 95% to 107% of prescription per ICRU 62.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Dose rests on **TE18** (20 Gy not inferior to 30 Gy) and field size on **TE10** (para-aortic over dog-leg for stage I). The authors concede the large trials used a **T11** superior border, so the T12 move is supported by mapping and an 80-pt series, not randomized data.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents clinical stage IA to IIB pure seminoma after inguinal orchiectomy, including pts with prior pelvic or scrotal surgery (classic dog-leg). Does not represent pts with horseshoe kidney, inflammatory bowel disease or prior RT, where chemotherapy is preferred.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Mapping defined a positive node as **1.0 cm short axis** on CT, so subcentimetre disease above L1 is invisible to it. Second-cancer gains are model-derived. 2012 vintage predates current surveillance and de-escalation practice.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The review favors **2D or 3D AP-PA over IMRT** because two fields give lower kidney, liver and bowel Dmean, even though IMRT spares marrow better. Proton cost-effectiveness vs photons or BEP x 3 is called controversial, not settled.

studies.interpretation:
The most durable part of this review is not the dose, which TE18 had already settled at 20 Gy in 10 fractions, but the geometry. Two border moves carry the paper: dropping the superior edge from the top of T11 to the top of T12, and lifting the dog-leg inferior edge from the obturator foramen to the top of the acetabulum. Both trade target volume for normal-tissue sparing in a population where nearly everyone is cured, so the burden of proof sits on toxicity rather than on control. That framing is right, but the evidence offered for each move deserves different weight.

The T12 recommendation leans on two sources. Bruns reported no relapses in the cranially reduced volume across 80 pts at a median follow-up of 7.1 years, and the Paly mapping of 69 clinical stage II pts found no positive node above L1. Neither is randomized, and the mapping counted only nodes reaching 1.0 cm in short axis on CT, which by construction cannot see the low-volume disease adjuvant RT is meant to sterilize. The authors themselves note that the large trials were run with a T11 border, which is a candid admission that the reduced field has never been tested at scale. The acetabular inferior border rests on an 87-pt German cohort with no pelvic relapses and on a consensus group endorsement; again consistent, again small.

The argument for staying with AP-PA rather than IMRT is the more interesting methodological choice. Seven-field IMRT lowers V75% and V100% for marrow, bowel, stomach, pancreas and liver, yet two fields deliver lower mean and median dose to the kidneys, liver and bowel. Because second-cancer risk in these organs is thought to track low-dose bath volume, the authors judge conformality a net loss here. That is a defensible inversion of the usual instinct, though the supporting risk estimates, including the 45% reduction attributed to the TE10 field shrinkage, come from a linear dose-response model rather than observed incidence.

What this does not settle is the larger question that now dominates stage I seminoma: whether adjuvant RT belongs in the pathway at all once surveillance is accepted. The review already places RT behind surveillance and, for likely non-compliers, behind carboplatin. Its practical value today is as a planning reference for the stage IIA/IIB pt who receives RT, and for the kidney constraints (each kidney D50% at or below 8 Gy on the dog-leg phase, 2 Gy on the boost) that give a concrete check on a plan. A reader should treat the borders as reasonable defaults supported by mapping, not as trial-validated volumes.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The parameters that transfer: superior border at top of T12 (no positive nodes above L1 among 69 mapped stage II pts), dog-leg inferior border at top of acetabulum (no pelvic relapses in 87 pts), and a vascular CTV of IVC + 1.2 cm and aorta + 1.9 cm, each trimming kidney, stomach or bowel dose.

open_questions: Does vascular-based 3D-CRT CTV lower late toxicity vs bony-anatomy fields?
Proton cost-effectiveness vs photons or BEP in stage II seminoma
Does the T12 superior border hold in larger prospective cohorts?

sites.intro: Rare late effect after central lung SABR: phrenic injury 2 yr out; authors suggest contouring the phrenic nerve as an OAR.

studies.name: Unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis after lung SABR (case report)
studies.tldr: Left hemidiaphragm paralysis 2y after 50 Gy/4fx lung SABR; phrenic-area Dmax 57.7 Gy (BED3 335.14 Gy), conservative mgmt, no local recurrence.
details: 🔍 Single case report: woman in her 50s, metastatic sinonasal adenoid cystic carcinoma, 2 lung mets
🔍 SABR 50 Gy/4 fx via VMAT, 4DCT sim, amplitude-based expiratory gating, daily CBCT
🔍 PTV 5 mm from GTV, limited to 3 mm into mediastinum for the LUL mass
📐 Phrenic-area Dmax 57.7 Gy (point dose to approximate location), BED3 335.14 Gy

subdetails: L hemidiaphragm elevation first visible on serial CT at 23 mo
Dyspnea + cough ~2 mo later, at 2 years; initially attributed to asthma
Sniff test confirmed L hemidiaphragmatic paralysis
Breathing exercises + ambulation → symptom improvement within 3 mo, no surgery
Paralysis persists on imaging; asymptomatic, no local recurrence at 38 mo

details.text: 🔗 Prospective central SABR trials cited by authors: no neuropathy reported, phrenic never contoured

details: ⚠️ Phrenic nerve not visible on CT; dose reconstructed retrospectively to an approximate location
⚠️ n=1; authors note other pts received higher doses without complications
⚠️ Prior L neck dissection + H&N RT; L vocal cord paresis attributed to vagus injury from that course

details.text: 🔍 Authors' planning mitigations for tumors abutting mediastinum
subdetails: Consider phrenic nerve as OAR along its course
Mediastinum outside PTV: max dose ≤ prescription dose
PTV/mediastinum overlap: ≤110% of prescription, V>105% kept small, GTV dose not compromised
No further dose reduction or coverage compromise advocated
Add phrenic injury to consent as a rare late effect

verdict.rationale: Single case report; one approximate point dose cannot define phrenic tolerance, and authors cite pts tolerating higher doses. Hypothesis-generating for contouring and surveillance only.
verdict.audience: Lung tumors abutting mediastinum along phrenic course, treated with SABR

studies.significance: The transferable detail is the authors' mediastinal constraint set, not the 57.7 Gy point: mediastinum outside PTV held to prescription dose, PTV/mediastinum overlap ≤110%, V>105% minimized. Injury occurred despite trimming the PTV to 3 mm into mediastinum, so this moves contouring and hotspot placement, not prescription.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a lung SABR target abutting the mediastinum along the phrenic course, this supports naming phrenic injury in consent and reading surveillance CTs for hemidiaphragm elevation; it does not support de-escalating dose or GTV coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-patient case report** from one institution with retrospective plan review by a radiation oncologist and thoracic radiologist. Follow-up to **38 months** after SABR.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Woman in her 50s with **metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma of the sinonasal tract**, 12 years from diagnosis. Prior resection with left neck dissection, adjuvant RT to sinuses and skull base, a VATS wedge resection, and multiple stereotactic courses; the **2 lung mets were the only known active disease**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **50 Gy in 4 fractions** to both lung mets via VMAT, 4DCT simulation, amplitude-based expiratory gating, daily CBCT. Uniform 5 mm PTV expansion, **limited to 3 mm into the mediastinum** for the LUL mass. Phrenic-area **Dmax 57.7 Gy, BED3 335.14 Gy**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Left hemidiaphragm elevation on CT at **23 months**, symptomatic dyspnea at 2 years, **sniff test confirmed paralysis**. Conservative management improved symptoms within 3 months; paralysis persists on imaging, **no local recurrence** at 38 months.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: **RTOG 0813** (120 pts, up to 60 Gy/5 fx), the **Indiana phase 2** (70 pts) and the authors' own **dose-adapted phase 2** (74 central tumors, up to 50 Gy/4 fx) reported no neuropathy. **None contoured the phrenic nerve**, so those trials could not have measured it.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents SABR-treated lung tumors abutting the mediastinum along the phrenic nerve course. Does not represent peripheral lung targets away from the mediastinum, or establish a phrenic dose threshold.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The nerve is not visible on CT, so the 57.7 Gy figure is a dose to an **approximate location**. Prior left neck dissection and head and neck RT are a competing exposure the report addresses only for the vocal cord paresis.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors frame the event as **likely underreported**: a diagnosis of exclusion, onset months to years out, and dyspnea easily attributed elsewhere. They propose **mediastinal hotspot control, consent and a rare-complication registry**, and explicitly **decline dose reduction**, given the cost of local failure.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this report is less the event itself than what it shows about how the field has ascertained toxicity in central lung SABR. The prospective series that define comfort with treating tumors near the mediastinum, RTOG 0813, the Indiana phase 2 and the Stanford dose-adapted phase 2, reported no neuropathy, but none contoured the phrenic nerve. Without a contour, a dose metric, or a planned review of the hemidiaphragm, the absence of events in those trials says as much about what was looked for as about how often it happens. The case shows how this toxicity looks in practice: a hemidiaphragm that rises quietly on surveillance CT, and dyspnea that the pt and clinicians first put down to asthma. That kind of event does not reach a trial toxicity form unless someone goes looking for it.

The dose number needs careful handling. The 57.7 Gy maximum is a point dose to the approximate area of a nerve that cannot be seen on CT, reconstructed after the event by a radiation oncologist and a thoracic radiologist. That adds localization uncertainty on top of the n=1 problem, and the authors concede that other pts received higher doses uneventfully. The sinoatrial node and recurrent laryngeal nerve series they cite show the same pattern: symptomatic and asymptomatic doses overlap, so dose alone does not sort pts. A reader should log this as one reported data point near the high end of what lands in the mediastinum with 50 Gy/4 fx, not as a tolerance. There is also a competing exposure. The pt had a left neck dissection and head and neck RT years earlier, and her left vocal cord paresis was attributed to that course. Serial CTs place the onset of diaphragm elevation after SABR, which argues for SABR as the cause, but a nerve already compromised by earlier treatment cannot be excluded and would make the case less generalizable.

What the report changes is narrow and sensible. The authors do not argue for lower prescriptions or weaker target coverage, and the outcome supports that: the lung mets were her only active disease, and local control held through 38 months. The proposed changes sit in planning and follow-up. Contour the mediastinum as a surrogate where the nerves can't be seen, keep hotspots out of it, mention the risk in consent, and read surveillance imaging for diaphragm position. Most of that costs nothing in tumor dose. The more interesting point is that this case already used a trimmed 3 mm mediastinal PTV margin and still produced the injury, so margin trimming alone may not protect the nerve when the GTV itself abuts it.

What would make this uninformative is a dose-response analysis across the many central targets already treated, showing no relationship between phrenic-region dose and diaphragm elevation. That analysis is feasible from existing plans and surveillance CTs. Until it exists, the honest position is that incidence is unknown and probably underestimated, and no dose threshold exists for clinicians to plan against.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable detail is the mediastinal constraint set: mediastinum outside PTV held to prescription dose, PTV/mediastinum overlap ≤110%, V>105% minimized. Injury occurred despite a 3 mm mediastinal PTV margin, so this moves contouring and hotspot placement for abutting targets, not the 50 Gy/4 fx prescription.

open_questions: Phrenic nerve dose-response threshold for SABR near the mediastinum
True incidence of SABR-induced phrenic injury, likely underreported
Optimal management: conservative care vs diaphragm plication

sites.intro: Dose and coverage framework for the tumor bed and elective cranial nerve pathways in PNI and PNTS, from 60 Gy adjuvant to 70 Gy gross PNTS.

studies.name: Perineural invasion and perineural tumor spread in head and neck cancer
studies.tldr: 60 Gy bed, 64-66 Gy close/positive margin, 50-60 Gy elective CN pathways, 70 Gy gross PNTS: expert target-volume framework for H&N PNI.

details.text: 📊 Disease control with RT reported in cited retrospective series

Unresectable/subtotally resected ACC, photon or particle: 36% to 93%
cSCC extensive PNI: 2y DSS 73% with RT vs DFS 40% unirradiated

studies.significance: The decision this moves is how far up the nerve to treat, not whether to irradiate: tumor bed alone for microscopic focal intratumoral PNI, retrograde CN pathway to the skull base at 50-60 Gy for ACC/SDC, extensive PNI, a named or >0.1 mm nerve, or a nerve margin. Interconnections (V2/VII via vidian and GSPN) are added only for PNTS.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected oral cavity SCC with PNI in small unnamed intratumoral nerves, this does not support CN pathway coverage to the skull base; that coverage is reserved for gross named nerve or CN involvement.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review with **author recommendations**, illustrated by 6 representative contoured cases. Not a systematic review; the authors state dose guidance rests on **limited and mostly empirically derived** data plus collective experience.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Mucosal SCC, cutaneous SCC and salivary malignancies (ACC, SDC, high-grade mucoepidermoid) with histologic **PNI** or imaging/clinical **PNTS**. PNI reported in **42% to 52%** of oral tongue/buccal SCC specimens and in **69%** of SDC.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Adjuvant bed **60 Gy**, **64-66 Gy** for close/positive margin, **50-60 Gy** to elective CN pathways with de-escalation toward 50 Gy near cochlea/brainstem, **70 Gy** to gross PNTS. Coverage runs **retrograde toward the skull base** by default; dose painting recommended; protons proposed to cut temporal lobe dose bath.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Skull-base coverage puts temporal lobe, cochlea, optic apparatus and brainstem at risk. Treating VII along the internal acoustic canal carries a **near-certain loss of hearing**; lower CN palsy is a common late effect, hence sparing uninvolved jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Builds on previously published contouring guidelines and the consensus NPC delineation guidelines, adding PNTS routes (foramen ovale, rotundum, vidian/GSPN) as privileged targets. For salivary cancers, concurrent cisplatin was deferred to Radiation Therapy Oncology Group clinical trial 1008, pending at publication.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents resected or unresectable H&N mucosal SCC, cutaneous SCC and salivary carcinoma with PNI or PNTS. Does not represent early oral cavity SCC with PNI as the sole adverse feature, where the adjuvant RT indication remains unsettled.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The cited cSCC benefit compares **DSS in irradiated vs DFS in unirradiated** pts. Histologic risk features (nerve caliber cut points of 0.1 or 1 mm, focal vs extensive) remain contested, and the authors note **no active clinical trials focused on PNI**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful output is a reproducible coverage ladder keyed to histology, PNI extent, nerve caliber, margin and imaging. Dose levels are convention plus anatomy, not dose-response; preclinical data that low-dose nerve RT suppresses PNI via GDNF hint elective volumes could be de-escalated, untested in pts.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this review to a radiation oncologist is not new evidence but a decision structure. Most departments improvise when a pathology report mentions perineural invasion: some treat the bed, some trace the nerve to the skull base, and the choice often depends on who contours the case. The authors convert that improvisation into a graded ladder, tumor bed alone, then retrograde elective coverage of the innervating cranial nerve, then communicating interconnections, then anterograde coverage, with each rung keyed to histology, extent of PNI, caliber of the involved nerve, margin along the nerve and imaging evidence of spread. The case atlas makes the ladder concrete for the sites where it matters most: V3 to foramen ovale for submandibular ACC, VII through the temporal bone for parotid disease, V2 to foramen rotundum for palate, the skull base foramina in T3-4 NPC.

The evidentiary footing is thin, and the authors say so. Dose guidance is described as limited and mostly empirically derived, drawn from retrospective series and collective experience. The outcome figures they cite illustrate why confidence should stay modest. The cutaneous SCC benefit is framed as a 2-year DSS of 73% in irradiated pts against a DFS of 40% in unirradiated pts, two different endpoints from a population selected into RT. Definitive RT control for unresectable ACC ranges from 36% to 93% across photon and particle series too heterogeneous to anchor a dose. The paper also concedes that PNI definitions were not standardized across the oral cavity literature, which may be why PNI predicts local failure in some series and not in others. The dose levels (60 Gy bed, 64-66 Gy for a close or positive margin, 50-60 Gy elective nerve, 70 Gy gross PNTS) are therefore conventional head and neck dose tiers applied to nerve anatomy, not a measured dose-response.

Against existing guidance, the review mostly extends rather than contradicts. For NPC it layers PNTS routes onto the consensus delineation guidelines. For oral cavity it pushes toward restraint, advising against routine skull-base nerve coverage unless gross named nerve or CN involvement is present, which is a useful check on reflexive volume expansion. On systemic therapy it is conservative: microscopic PNI alone does not justify concurrent therapy in resected mucosal SCC, and the salivary question was deferred to Radiation Therapy Oncology Group clinical trial 1008, pending when this was written. Readers should treat that section as dated.

What would make the framework wrong is an overestimate of occult centripetal spread. Elective skull-base coverage trades cochlear, temporal lobe and lower cranial nerve toxicity for protection against an uncommon but catastrophic failure. If more sensitive imaging showed occult nerve involvement to be rarer than assumed, the elective volumes would shrink, and the authors anticipate exactly that. The preclinical finding that low-dose nerve irradiation suppressed invasion through reduced GDNF suggests the elective dose itself may be higher than needed, but that remains untested in pts. Until a trial addresses PNI directly, and the authors note none was active, this is the best available map rather than a validated one.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The decision this moves is how far up the nerve to treat: tumor bed alone for microscopic focal intratumoral PNI, retrograde CN pathway to the skull base at 50-60 Gy for ACC/SDC, extensive PNI, a named or >0.1 mm nerve, or a nerve margin. Interconnections are added only for PNTS.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Per the authors, microscopic PNI alone in resected mucosal SCC is not an indication for concurrent systemic therapy. Concurrent platinum or cetuximab is considered for symptomatic nerve invasion or unresected gross PNTS; cisplatin with postop RT in high-risk salivary cancers awaited Radiation Therapy Oncology Group clinical trial 1008 at publication.

open_questions: Independent prognostic weight of PNI histologic features
Concurrent cisplatin with postop RT in high-risk salivary cancers
Adjuvant RT for early oral cavity SCC with PNI alone

⚠️ Cross-trial overlays (Figs 1-2) mix populations, agents, durations and time zeros
studies.significance: The RT argument is biological: at low pre-SRT PSA, recurrence is likely confined to bed or pelvis, where 64 to 72 Gy treats microscopic disease, so ADT adds little; above PSA 0.7, micrometastatic spread makes systemic therapy necessary. RTOG 9601's bicalutamide OS HR moved from 1.13 below 0.7 to 0.45 above 1.5.
studies.monday_clinic: In a post-prostatectomy man with pre-SRT PSA 0.1-0.5 and grade group 1-3, this framework supports salvage RT alone; it does not extend to PSA above 1.0, where every grade group maps to STADT or LTADT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-author **expert review** in Q&A format (Red Journal), weighing **RTOG 9601** and **GETUG-AFU-16** and applying a simplified multicenter consensus framework. No new patient data.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Early SRT is framed as targeting disease confined to the **prostate bed and/or pelvis**, where microscopic disease is treated with **64 to 72 Gy**. Above PSA 0.7, micrometastatic or imaging-visible disease becomes likely and RT alone undertreats.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 9601 (bicalutamide, mostly late SRT) and GETUG-AFU-16 (6 mo GnRH agonist, mostly early SRT) are the randomized trials weighed; per the author, neither showed **DM or OS benefit in early SRT**. RADICALS-HD and SPPORT post-date the piece and are not addressed.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-prostatectomy men with a rising PSA considered for salvage RT. Does not represent persistently elevated postoperative PSA or node-positive disease, both routed to trials.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Early vs late SRT is defined differently across trials (**0.7 in RTOG 9601, 0.5 in GETUG-AFU-16**), so the early-SRT read is stitched from two non-matching cut points. The author concedes that PSA-based frameworks **ignore tumor biology**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The durable point is the endpoint: biochemical control after a GnRH agonist is partly testosterone suppression, so a BCR gain does not show **clinically meaningful benefit**. The grid is a dated snapshot of thresholds and should be read against newer randomized salvage data.

studies.interpretation:
The argument rests on one observation: in RTOG 9601, pre-SRT PSA behaved as a predictive marker for bicalutamide, not only a prognostic one. The OS hazard ratio moved from 1.13 below PSA 0.7 to 0.45 above 1.5, and the absolute OS effect went from a 4.1% decrement to a 24.6% gain. If that gradient is real, the trial that established hormone therapy with salvage RT was mostly answering a question about late salvage. Only about 10% of its men had PSA at or below 0.3, and PSA below 0.5 was excluded for much of accrual. GETUG-AFU-16, the trial that enrolled the early-salvage population, used 6 months of a GnRH agonist and, as the author reads it, showed no metastasis or survival benefit.

The weak point is that the gradient comes from a subgroup interaction in a single trial. The source does not say whether the PSA cut points were prespecified, and 0.7 and 1.5 are not natural biological thresholds. A positive interaction test is more persuasive than a subgroup p-value on its own, but one trial's interaction still needs replication before it decides who gets ADT. The cross-trial reasoning is looser. Overlaying RTOG 9408 intermediate-risk intact-prostate curves on RTOG 9601, and lining up absolute improvements across four disease states, mixes populations, agents, durations and time zeros. The figure works as an illustration that short ADT buys a biochemical gain of about 10% even in low-risk intact disease. It is not a quantitative comparison.

The endpoint argument is the strongest part of the piece. Biochemical control measured after a GnRH agonist is partly a pharmacologic artifact, because testosterone stays subnormal for 6 to 12 months after the course ends. The author cites ICECaP, pooling over 28,000 men, as supporting distant metastasis rather than biochemical recurrence as the survival surrogate. For an RT reader this reframes GETUG-AFU-16. A 12% crude biochemical benefit below PSA 0.5 is close to what short ADT gives any prostate-confined disease. The 36% figure above 0.5 is where a systemic effect plausibly begins, which fits the radiobiologic case that early SRT at 64 to 72 Gy already treats the disease that matters.

The piece is a 2018 position. It predates RADICALS-HD and SPPORT, which addressed hormone duration and pelvic nodal coverage in the salvage setting, and it predates routine PSMA PET restaging before salvage RT at low PSA. Its own caveat still holds: PSA-and-grade frameworks ignore tumor biology, which is why NRG GU-006 was designed as a biomarker-stratified trial of apalutamide in mostly early SRT, capped at PSA 1.0.

What it changes for the RT decision is narrow. For grade group 1 to 3 at PSA 0.1 to 0.5, the grid supports SRT alone. It leaves open the high-grade, low-PSA man, whom it flags for a discussion rather than a default, and it sends node-positive and persistent-PSA patients to trials. Read the grid as a snapshot of where thresholds sat before the newer randomized salvage data, and check it against those data before using it to withhold ADT.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Early SRT at 64 to 72 Gy is framed as already treating bed and pelvic microscopic disease, so ADT adds little at low PSA. The grid supports SRT alone for grade group 1-3 at PSA 0.1-0.5, with ADT for every grade group above PSA 1.0.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Antiandrogen benefit concentrates in late salvage: RTOG 9601's bicalutamide OS HR was 1.13 below PSA 0.7 and 0.45 above 1.5. Escalation is being tested on an ADT backbone (FORMULA-509, RTOG 3506), and docetaxel in NRG GU-002 for persistent PSA ≥0.2.

studies.name: Moderate hypofractionation for prostate cancer: a user's guide
studies.tldr: 60 Gy/20 fx preferred: PROFIT, CHHiP and NRG Oncology 0415 show 5-yr non-inferiority for disease control and late toxicity in localised prostate cancer.
details: 📊 Three large RCTs: moderate hypofx non-inferior for disease control, late toxicity and PROMs at 5 yr
📊 5-yr biochemical-clinical FFS in the order of 85% to 90% across all three trials
📊 Late G≥3 toxicity 1%-4% across the three trials, regardless of schedule

details.text: 📊 PMH phase 2, 60 Gy/20 fx, >10 yr f/u
subdetails: Any G3: 2%
G≥2 GI: 4% at 5 yr, unchanged at 8 yr
G≥2 GU: 9% at 5 yr, 12% at 8 yr; many events transient

details: ⚠️ NRG 0415 hypofx arm carried higher BED (128 vs 118 Gy, α/β 3) → small rise in late G2 GI/GU
⚠️ HYPRO 64.6 Gy/19 fx (EQD2 90 Gy prostate, 83 Gy normal tissue) → unfavourable toxicity
🔍 Elective nodal RT not evaluated in any large hypofx trial
🔍 CHHiP excluded upper-end high risk (Gleason ≥9, Gleason 8 with T3 or PSA >10, among others)

details.text: 🔍 Relative contraindications: authors call none firm
subdetails: Baseline IPSS >12: worse GU function in FCCC post hoc subgroup only, not confirmed in larger trials
Prior TURP: not excluded in any large trial; 8% of CHHiP
Gland size: no exclusion if dose-volume constraints can be met
Anticoagulation: excluded in CHHiP only

details: 🔍 IMRT/VMAT + daily IGRT; CTV-PTV ~7 mm, 3 to 5 mm with intrafraction monitoring

details.text: 📐 Authors' modified ideal aims (whole-organ OARs, 7 mm PTV)
subdetails: Bladder neck/urethra: Dmax ≤ 61 Gy
PTV/rectum gradient: 57 to 30 Gy in ≤10 mm (acceptable ≤15 mm)

details: 🔗 Arcangeli 62 Gy/20 vs 80 Gy/40 fx, 168 high-risk pts: 10-yr FFBF 72% vs 65% (p = 0.148)
studies.significance: The practical payload is the planning envelope: CTV-PTV ~7 mm with daily IGRT, urethra/bladder neck Dmax ≤ 61 Gy, and the 57 to 30 Gy gradient within ≤10 mm at the rectal interface. Prior TURP and large glands were never trial exclusions, so they don't by themselves argue for conventional fractionation if constraints are met.
studies.monday_clinic: In localised low- or intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated to the prostate alone, this supports 60 Gy/20 fx over 74 Gy/37 or 78 Gy/39 fx; it does not extend to elective pelvic nodal RT or the very high-risk group CHHiP excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review with practical planning guidance (JMIRO 2018). Seven randomised moderate-hypofx trials reported to date; the argument centres on **PROFIT, CHHiP and NRG Oncology 0415**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **60 Gy/20 fx preferred.** IMRT/VMAT with daily IGRT; CTV-PTV margin in the order of **7 mm**, down to **3 to 5 mm** with intrafraction monitoring. Proximal SV per PROFIT (1 cm if SV risk >15%) or CHHiP (2 cm if <15%, entire SV if >15%).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Intermediate risk dominated; high risk was **12% of CHHiP**, with the upper end excluded. Prior TURP (8% of CHHiP) and gland size were not exclusions; anticoagulation was excluded in CHHiP only. Authors treat **none as a firm contraindication**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: HYPRO (64.6 Gy/19 vs 78 Gy/39 fx, 804 pts) is framed as a dose-too-high cautionary tale, not a fractionation failure. NRG 0415's small late G2 excess is attributed to its higher BED (128 vs 118 Gy).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents localised low-, intermediate- and selected high-risk prostate cancer treated to the prostate with or without SV, no nodal RT. Does not represent elective pelvic nodal RT or the Gleason ≥9 / very high-risk group CHHiP excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Core trials had **median f/u 5-6 years** while late GU toxicity keeps accruing past 5 years. Published 2018, so HYPO-RT-PC was preliminary (abstract only) and PACE ongoing.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors argue patient selection, ADT integration and technique matter more than modest dose-fractionation differences. Main support: CHHiP GI toxicity around **50% lower** than MRC RT01.

studies.interpretation:
The case this guide makes rests less on any single trial than on convergence. PROFIT, CHHiP and NRG Oncology 0415 used different comparators, different risk mixes and different ADT policies (none permitted in PROFIT, 3-6 months in CHHiP), yet all three hazard ratios sit below 1.0 (0.96, 0.84, 0.85). When three designs that disagree on that much land on the same side of unity, the non-inferiority conclusion is hard to pin on a quirk of one protocol. The authors lean further on the dose-escalation literature: large gains in biochemical control from escalation never became survival differences, so a late divergence in disease control from a modest change in dose per fraction would be surprising. That is a reasonable inference, but it is an argument by analogy, not an observation.

The toxicity story is more instructive than the efficacy story, because that is where the trials diverged. NRG Oncology 0415 saw a small rise in late grade 2 GI and GU events, and its hypofractionated arm carried a higher BED than its control (128 vs 118 Gy at α/β 3). HYPRO pushed further, 64.6 Gy in 19 fractions, an EQD2 of 83 Gy for normal tissue, and paid for it in toxicity. Read together, these suggest the toxicity cost tracks how far the normal-tissue dose is pushed rather than hypofractionation itself, which is why the guide anchors on 60 Gy in 20 fractions and not a more aggressive schedule. The CHHiP observation that GI toxicity ran around 50% lower than in MRC RT01 points the same way: technique and image guidance appear to move toxicity more than the schedule does, and the planning aims the authors publish are the operational expression of that view.

Confidence should drop at the edges of the enrolled populations. Intermediate risk dominated all three trials. High-risk disease was 12% of CHHiP, and that trial excluded the upper end of the spectrum because 6 months of ADT was judged insufficient. No large trial treated pelvic nodes, so a hypofractionated whole-pelvis plan has no randomised support in this body of evidence. The pre-treatment LUTS concern comes from a post hoc FCCC subgroup (IPSS >12) never reproduced in the larger trials; it is weak evidence of harm, but also weak reassurance, since the large trials were not designed to look for it.

Follow-up maturity is the remaining honest objection, and the authors concede it. Median follow-up periods of 5-6 years are short for late GU toxicity, which keeps accruing. The Princess Margaret phase 2 data partly answer this for 60 Gy in 20 fractions (any grade 3 at 2% beyond 10 years, grade ≥2 GU 9% at 5 years and 12% at 8 years), but from a single centre. As a 2018 piece, the guide also predates mature reporting from HYPO-RT-PC and PACE, so its treatment of extreme hypofractionation is a snapshot of open questions rather than a position. The durable contribution is narrower: a defensible default schedule, a list of relative contraindications that the trials did not actually exclude, and dose-volume targets a department can adopt.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The practical payload is the planning envelope: CTV-PTV ~7 mm with daily IGRT, urethra/bladder neck Dmax ≤ 61 Gy, and the 57 to 30 Gy gradient within ≤10 mm at the rectal interface. Prior TURP and large glands were never trial exclusions, so they don't by themselves argue for conventional fractionation if constraints are met.

papers.journal: Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology
papers.abstract: Summary Three large randomised controlled trials have been published in the last year demonstrating the non‐inferiority of moderate hypofractionation compared to conventional fractionation for localised prostate cancer with respect to both disease control and late toxicity at 5 years. Furthermore, no clinically significant differences in patient‐reported outcomes have emerged. More mature follow‐up data are now also available from phase 2 studies confirming that moderate hypofractionation is associated with low rates of significant toxicity at 10 years. Moving forward it is likely that appropriate patient selection, integration of androgen deprivation and attention to optimising technique will play a more important role than modest differences in dose‐fractionation schedules. Here we briefly review the evidence, discuss issues of patient selection and provide an approach to implementing moderately hypofractionated radiation therapy for prostate cancer in clinical practice.
